title: Conditions of the Ovary
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the common non-neoplastic conditions of the ovary and adnexa: functional cysts, paraovarian cysts, ovarian torsion, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and tubo-ovarian cysts and abscesses. Each is explained from the normal ovarian cycle, adnexal anatomy, or the spread of pelvic infection. Board questions usually give an adnexal mass in a particular setting (pregnancy, a molar gestation, fever after PID, sudden pain during exercise) or a woman with irregular cycles and hirsutism, and ask for the mechanism or the expected complication. If you know which hormone drives each cyst, why veins close before arteries in torsion, and how LH and insulin together produce androgen excess, most of these questions follow.
prerequisites: The ovarian cycle: follicular phase, ovulation, corpus luteum, and luteolysis (RE-7)
The two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of ovarian steroid synthesis
Anatomy of the broad ligament, mesovarium, mesosalpinx, and the ovarian and uterine arteries
Embryology of the mesonephric (Wolffian) and paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts
Insulin signaling and the concept of insulin resistance

connections.how: The very high hCG of a hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma is what produces bilateral theca lutein cysts.
Chronic anovulation in PCOS leaves the endometrium under estrogen without progesterone, the main driver of endometrioid carcinoma.
Insulin resistance links PCOS to type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, fatty liver, and acanthosis nigricans.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis start the ascending infection that ends in a tubo-ovarian abscess and tubal infertility.
Both torsions obstruct low-pressure veins before arteries, so the gonad swells and then undergoes hemorrhagic infarction.

terms.def: An ovarian cyst formed by an exaggeration of the normal cycle (follicle or corpus luteum) rather than by neoplasia, which usually regresses on its own.
A fluid-filled cyst formed when a maturing follicle fails to rupture at ovulation and continues to enlarge.
A cyst formed when the corpus luteum fails to regress and fills with fluid or blood after ovulation.
Multiple, usually bilateral ovarian cysts with luteinized theca cells, caused by very high hCG stimulating the LH receptor.
The structures beside the uterus: ovaries, uterine tubes, and the ligaments and vessels that support them.
The suspensory ligament of the ovary, a peritoneal fold from the pelvic sidewall that carries the ovarian artery, vein, lymphatics, and nerves.
The part of the broad ligament between the uterine tube and the mesovarium, where paraovarian cysts and embryonic duct remnants lie.
Excess androgen action, shown clinically by hirsutism, acne, or scalp hair loss, or biochemically by raised total or free testosterone.
A liver-made plasma protein that binds testosterone and estradiol with high affinity, so its level sets the free, active hormone fraction.
Estrogen acting on the endometrium without the cyclic progesterone that normally converts it to secretory endometrium and leads to orderly shedding.
A walled-off collection of pus involving an inflamed uterine tube adherent to the ovary, usually a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease.
A uterine tube distended with clear fluid after its fimbrial end has been sealed by scarring from earlier infection.

sections.title: Functional cysts: follicular, corpus luteum, and theca lutein

blocks.text: Functional cysts are the commonest adnexal masses in women of reproductive age. They are not tumors but exaggerations of normal ovarian events, so each type is best recognized by the hormone that drives it and the phase of the cycle in which it forms. A normal dominant follicle reaches about 2 to 2.5 cm before ovulation; a fluid-filled structure larger than about 3 cm is usually called a cyst. Functional cysts are lined by granulosa or luteinized cells, are usually simple and unilocular on ultrasound, and most resolve within one to three cycles.
Follicular cyst

When the midcycle LH surge fails to trigger rupture, the follicle keeps accumulating fluid. Its granulosa cells may continue to aromatize theca androgen into estradiol, so a follicular cyst can produce estrogen. Persistent estrogen without a following luteal phase can cause irregular bleeding and, if prolonged, endometrial hyperplasia. In girls, an autonomously functioning follicular cyst causes gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) precocious puberty, the mechanism seen in McCune-Albright syndrome.
Corpus luteum cyst

After ovulation, capillaries grow into the former follicle to supply the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone. This vascular, thin-walled structure bleeds easily, and if it fails to regress it becomes a cyst filled with fluid or blood (hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst). Continued progesterone secretion can delay menses. Rupture, often after intercourse or exercise, releases blood into the peritoneum, causing sudden unilateral pain and hemoperitoneum that mimics a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; anticoagulation raises the risk. A corpus luteum cyst is also normal in early pregnancy, where it is maintained by hCG.
Theca lutein cysts

hCG and LH share an alpha subunit and have closely related beta subunits, so hCG activates the LH receptor on theca cells. When hCG is far above normal, theca cells in many follicles luteinize and the follicles fill with fluid, giving multiple, usually bilateral cysts that can enlarge both ovaries considerably. The causes are complete hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation, and ovarian hyperstimulation with exogenous gonadotropins. Because theca cells make androgen, these cysts occasionally cause maternal virilization. They regress as hCG falls, for example after a mole is evacuated.

blocks.caption: Each cyst matches the hormone environment in which it forms. Bilateral, multiple cysts point to an hCG source.

blocks.title: Bilateral cysts in a large-for-dates pregnancy
blocks.text: A woman at 12 weeks has vaginal bleeding, a uterus large for dates, severe vomiting, and bilateral multiloculated adnexal masses. Start with the cysts: bilateral and multiple means hCG-driven, so the question becomes why hCG is so high. Hyperemesis fits very high hCG, and a uterus large for dates with bleeding fits a complete hydatidiform mole (multiple gestation is the other common cause, and ultrasound separates them). The cysts are theca lutein cysts, not tumors, and should regress as hCG falls after the mole is removed. A persistently rising hCG would suggest persistent trophoblastic disease rather than an ovarian problem.

The ovary is suspended at two points. Laterally, the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament runs from the pelvic sidewall and carries the ovarian artery, vein, lymphatics, and nerves. Medially, the ovarian ligament (utero-ovarian ligament) joins the ovary to the uterus, and the ovarian branch of the uterine artery runs with it to anastomose with the ovarian artery. Ovarian torsion is rotation of the ovary, usually with the tube (adnexal torsion), around the axis formed by these two attachments, which twists the vascular pedicle.

A normal adult ovary is small and rarely twists. Torsion usually needs a lever: a cyst or tumor, often about 5 cm or larger, makes the ovary heavy and mobile. Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a classic lead point, and functional cysts, ovaries enlarged by hyperstimulation, and pregnancy also predispose. Malignant tumors twist less often, probably because invasion and adhesions fix them in place. In prepubertal girls a normal ovary can twist because its ligaments are relatively long. Torsion is more often right-sided, a pattern usually attributed to the sigmoid colon occupying and stabilizing the left pelvis.

blocks.title: Ovarian torsion: from twist to infarction
steps: Enlarged ovary or mass acts as a lever
Adnexa rotate around the vascular pedicle
Low-pressure veins and lymphatics compress first
Arterial inflow continues; ovary swells with edema and congestion
Rising tissue pressure finally blocks arterial inflow
Hemorrhagic infarction and necrosis
blocks.caption: Outflow fails before inflow, so the ovary enlarges and becomes congested before it infarcts.

blocks.text: The sequence follows from vessel wall structure. Veins and lymphatics have thin walls and low pressure, so a partial twist collapses them while the thick-walled, high-pressure artery stays open. Blood keeps entering but cannot leave, so the ovary becomes edematous, congested, and enlarged, which further tightens the twist. When interstitial pressure exceeds arterial pressure, inflow stops and hemorrhagic infarction follows.

The ischemic, stretched capsule produces sudden, severe, unilateral pelvic or lower abdominal pain, often during exertion, with nausea and vomiting from visceral afferent stimulation. The twist may be intermittent, giving episodes of pain that resolve and recur. Low-grade fever and leukocytosis suggest necrosis. Ultrasound shows an enlarged, edematous ovary, often with follicles pushed to the periphery and a twisted pedicle (whirlpool sign). Doppler may show absent flow, but normal flow does not exclude torsion: the dual arterial supply and partial or intermittent twisting can preserve some flow early.

blocks.predict: Why does a twisted ovary become larger before it becomes infarcted, and why can Doppler still show arterial flow?
blocks.explain: Thin-walled, low-pressure veins collapse first while the artery keeps delivering blood, so the ovary swells with trapped blood and edema. Arterial flow persists until tissue pressure exceeds arterial pressure, and the ovary also receives blood from the uterine artery through the ovarian ligament.

blocks.text: Paraovarian (paratubal) cysts lie in the broad ligament, usually in the mesosalpinx between the uterine tube and the ovary, and are separate from the ovary itself. They are thin-walled, unilocular, and filled with clear fluid. They are common, are found at any age, and most are small, benign, and asymptomatic.

Their origin is embryologic. In the female embryo the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts form the tubes, uterus, and upper vagina, while the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts regress because there is no testosterone to maintain them. Regression is incomplete, and small remnants persist in the broad ligament. Cysts can arise from these mesonephric remnants, from paramesonephric remnants, or from inclusions of peritoneal mesothelium.

blocks.title: Embryonic remnants near the ovary
blocks.caption: Mesonephric remnants persist in the broad ligament and along the lateral vagina, which is why cysts can form beside, rather than within, the ovary.

blocks.text: Because the cyst arises outside the ovary, imaging shows a normal ovary, with its own follicles, beside the cyst, and the cyst does not change with the menstrual cycle the way a functional cyst does. This is the key distinction from an ovarian cyst. A paraovarian cyst also lacks the hormone-producing cells of a functional cyst, so it causes no endocrine effects.

Complications come from size and mobility. A large cyst can act as a lever for torsion of the cyst itself, the tube, or the whole adnexa, with the same venous-then-arterial sequence as ovarian torsion and the same sudden pain. Hemorrhage into the cyst or rupture causes acute pain. Large cysts can also press on the bladder or bowel. Neoplasms arising in paraovarian cysts are rare.

sections.title: PCOS pathogenesis: gonadotropins, insulin, and follicle arrest

blocks.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder of women of reproductive age, affecting roughly 6 to 13% depending on the criteria used. It is a syndrome of chronic anovulation and androgen excess, not a disease of cysts: the cysts are arrested follicles. Its pathogenesis is easiest to follow through the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model.

blocks.title: The two-cell, two-gonadotropin model and what goes wrong in PCOS
rows: LH (with insulin as cofactor) drives cholesterol to androgens, mainly androstenedione, via CYP17
High LH and high insulin raise CYP17 activity and androgen output
FSH induces aromatase (CYP19), converting theca androgen to estradiol
Relatively low FSH and high AMH limit aromatase, so androgen accumulates
Insulin suppresses SHBG synthesis, raising free testosterone
More substrate and more fat give steady estrone
blocks.caption: Androgen production outpaces conversion to estradiol, and low SHBG increases the free fraction that reaches tissues.

blocks.text: The neuroendocrine defect is a rapid GnRH pulse frequency. Fast pulses favor transcription of the LH beta subunit, while slow pulses favor FSH, so LH rises and FSH stays normal or low; the LH to FSH ratio is often above 2 to 1, although it is not a diagnostic criterion. Pulses stay fast partly because the hypothalamus is less sensitive to progesterone negative feedback and partly because anovulation means little progesterone is made.

Insulin resistance is present in a large proportion of women with PCOS, including lean women, and obesity worsens it. The resistance is selective: glucose uptake in muscle and fat is impaired, but the ovary and liver still respond to the compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Insulin acts with LH on theca cells to increase androgen synthesis and lowers hepatic SHBG, so free testosterone rises even when total testosterone is only mildly raised.

blocks.title: PCOS: from gonadotropin imbalance to anovulation
steps: Rapid GnRH pulses raise LH relative to FSH
LH and insulin drive theca androgen overproduction
Low FSH limits granulosa aromatase
Insulin lowers SHBG; free testosterone rises
Intraovarian androgen arrests small antral follicles
No dominant follicle, no ovulation, no corpus luteum
No progesterone; estrogen acts unopposed
blocks.caption: Two inputs, high LH and high insulin, converge on the theca cell; the androgen-rich follicle then fails to mature.

blocks.text: Within the ovary, high androgen and high anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) from the many small follicles reduce FSH responsiveness, so no follicle is selected as dominant. Follicles stall at about 2 to 9 mm and line up beneath a thickened, fibrotic cortex, giving the peripheral string of pearls on ultrasound, with hyperplastic theca and stroma. Without ovulation no corpus luteum forms, so progesterone stays low and GnRH pulses stay fast, which closes a self-sustaining loop.

blocks.title: The self-sustaining loop of PCOS
steps: Fast GnRH pulses raise LH
LH and insulin raise ovarian androgen
Androgen arrests follicles; no ovulation
No corpus luteum, so little progesterone
Weak progesterone feedback keeps GnRH pulses fast
blocks.caption: Anovulation removes the progesterone signal that would normally slow GnRH pulses, so the disorder perpetuates itself.

blocks.predict: Why is free testosterone often more abnormal than total testosterone in PCOS?
blocks.explain: Hyperinsulinemia suppresses hepatic SHBG. With less binding protein, a larger fraction of testosterone circulates free and active, so androgen effects appear even when total testosterone is near normal.
blocks.check: The liver row of the two-cell table and the paragraph on insulin resistance.

sections.title: PCOS: findings and complications explained by mechanism

blocks.text: Every finding in PCOS traces back to one of three disturbances: androgen excess, anovulation with unopposed estrogen, or insulin resistance. The commonly used Rotterdam criteria require two of three features (oligo-ovulation or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound) after other causes are excluded. Because polycystic-appearing ovaries are common in healthy young women, ultrasound alone never establishes PCOS.

blocks.title: PCOS findings and their mechanisms
rows: Follicle arrest prevents ovulation; bleeding is irregular breakthrough of proliferative endometrium
Anovulation; the most common cause of anovulatory infertility
Androgen, converted to DHT by 5-alpha reductase in the hair follicle, turns vellus into terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas
Acne and male-pattern scalp hair thinning
Androgen enlarges sebaceous glands and raises sebum; DHT shortens the growth phase of scalp follicles
Common but not universal; visceral fat worsens insulin resistance and adds estrone
Very high insulin stimulates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts, giving velvety dark skin in folds
Type 2 diabetes and impaired glucose tolerance
Insulin resistance until beta cells can no longer compensate
Insulin resistance increases lipolysis and fatty acid flow to the liver: high triglycerides and VLDL, low HDL
Chronic estrogen without progesterone drives unchecked proliferation (endometrioid type)
blocks.caption: Androgen excess explains the skin findings, anovulation explains the cycle and endometrial findings, and insulin resistance explains the metabolic findings.

blocks.text: The endometrial risk deserves special attention. In a normal cycle, progesterone from the corpus luteum stops estrogen-driven proliferation, converts the endometrium to a secretory pattern, and its withdrawal causes orderly shedding. In PCOS, estrone from adipose aromatization and estradiol from arrested follicles provide steady, moderate estrogen with no luteal progesterone. The endometrium keeps proliferating without regular shedding, progressing to hyperplasia and, in some women, endometrioid adenocarcinoma at a younger age than usual.

Other associations follow the same mechanisms: nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnea through insulin resistance and obesity, and gestational diabetes when pregnancy adds its own insulin resistance. Laboratory findings typically include raised free testosterone, low SHBG, raised LH with normal or low FSH, and high AMH; estradiol is usually in the normal early follicular range rather than high.

PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion because other disorders share its features. Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency raises 17-hydroxyprogesterone, hyperprolactinemia and thyroid disease disturb ovulation, and Cushing syndrome adds insulin resistance and hirsutism. An androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumor is suggested by rapid onset, very high testosterone or DHEAS, and frank virilization (clitoromegaly, deepened voice), which PCOS rarely causes.

blocks.title: Linking a PCOS presentation to its mechanisms
blocks.text: A 24-year-old has 5 periods a year, hirsutism, acne, BMI 33, and dark velvety skin on her neck. Free testosterone is high, total testosterone mildly raised, SHBG low, and LH to FSH about 3 to 1. The cycle history shows anovulation. The low SHBG and dark neck skin show hyperinsulinemia, which both suppresses SHBG and stimulates IGF-1 receptors in skin. The high LH explains theca androgen excess, and the free fraction is high because SHBG is low. Because she rarely ovulates, her endometrium is under estrogen without progesterone, so she carries a long-term risk of endometrial hyperplasia, and her insulin resistance puts her at risk of type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia.

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is ascending infection of the upper genital tract: endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, and pelvic peritonitis. It usually begins with Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis infecting the endocervix. Cervical mucus and the closed cervix normally keep vaginal bacteria out; once the endocervical barrier is damaged, and especially around menses when the cervix opens and mucus thins, organisms ascend to the endometrium and tubes. The infection then becomes polymicrobial, joined by vaginal anaerobes (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus), gram-negative rods such as Escherichia coli, and organisms associated with bacterial vaginosis.

blocks.title: From cervical infection to tubo-ovarian abscess
steps: Gonococcal or chlamydial endocervicitis
Ascent to endometrium and tubes (salpingitis)
Mixed flora, including anaerobes, join the infection
Inflamed tube and fimbriae adhere to the ovary
Pus collects in a walled-off tubo-ovarian abscess
Rupture spills pus into the peritoneum
blocks.caption: Ascending infection becomes polymicrobial and is walled off against the ovary; rupture converts a localized abscess into generalized peritonitis.

blocks.text: In the tube, gonococci damage ciliated cells (partly through lipooligosaccharide and peptidoglycan fragments that induce TNF), and chlamydial infection provokes a chronic immune response with marked scarring, often with few acute symptoms. Purulent exudate from the fimbriae bathes the ovary, and fibrin binds the inflamed tube and ovary into one mass, the tubo-ovarian complex. When pus collects in a walled-off cavity within this mass, a tubo-ovarian abscess forms; anaerobes thrive in its low-oxygen interior. Women with an intrauterine device have a classic association with Actinomyces israelii abscesses.

The manifestations follow the inflammation: lower abdominal pain, fever above 38.3 °C (101 °F), cervical motion and adnexal tenderness from inflamed peritoneum, purulent cervical discharge, a tender adnexal mass, leukocytosis, and raised C-reactive protein and ESR. Spread along the paracolic gutter to the liver capsule causes perihepatitis with right upper quadrant pain (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). Rupture of the abscess spills pus into the peritoneal cavity, producing generalized peritonitis, a rigid abdomen, and septic shock.

blocks.title: Late sequelae of PID and their mechanisms
rows: Scarring blocks the lumen or destroys fimbriae, so the ovum cannot be captured or transported
Partial damage to cilia and mucosal folds slows transport, so the embryo implants in the tube
Fimbrial end seals; tubal secretions accumulate as clear fluid
After infection resolves, the adherent tube and ovary leave a sterile fluid-filled cavity
Adhesions bind pelvic organs and stretch on movement
blocks.caption: Healing by fibrosis, not active infection, explains most long-term consequences.

blocks.text: The distinction between a tubo-ovarian cyst and abscess is clinical and microbiological. An abscess is an active infection with fever and leukocytosis; a tubo-ovarian cyst is the sterile, fluid-filled remnant of an earlier one. Both differ from a hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst, which gives sudden pain without fever, and from torsion, which gives abrupt pain in a previously well woman.

blocks.predict: A woman treated for PID five years ago now has a positive pregnancy test and unilateral pelvic pain at 7 weeks. Why is her risk of ectopic pregnancy raised?
blocks.explain: PID scars the tubal mucosa and destroys cilia. A partly damaged tube still lets sperm reach the ovum but transports the larger embryo too slowly, so it implants in the tube.
blocks.check: The table of late sequelae of PID.

integration.text: Physiology and anatomy explain most ovarian conditions. Functional cysts are the follicle and corpus luteum of the normal cycle carried too far, and theca lutein cysts follow from hCG acting on the LH receptor, linking the ovary to gestational trophoblastic disease. Adnexal anatomy explains torsion, since the ovary hangs on a vascular pedicle and an enlarged ovary twists it, and embryology explains paraovarian cysts as embryonic duct remnants beside a normal ovary. The same venous-before-arterial obstruction that infarcts a twisted ovary also infarcts a twisted testis.

PCOS joins reproductive endocrinology to biochemistry and metabolism. The two-cell model, GnRH pulse frequency, SHBG binding, and peripheral aromatization explain its androgen excess and anovulation, while selective insulin resistance explains acanthosis nigricans, diabetes, and dyslipidemia, and unopposed estrogen explains endometrial carcinoma. Microbiology and pathology complete the chapter: gonorrhea and chlamydia start PID, mixed anaerobes form the abscess, and fibrosis produces infertility and ectopic pregnancy. These conditions overlap in practice, since any adnexal mass can twist and several cause sudden pelvic pain, so the setting (pregnancy, fever, metabolic features) is often what separates them.

summary: Follicular cysts are unruptured follicles that may secrete estrogen; corpus luteum cysts may make progesterone and can bleed and rupture into the peritoneum, mimicking ectopic pregnancy.
Bilateral, multiple theca lutein cysts mean very high hCG (mole, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation, hyperstimulation) acting on theca LH receptors, and they regress as hCG falls.
Ovarian torsion needs a lever, usually a mass about 5 cm or larger such as a mature cystic teratoma; veins close before arteries, so the ovary swells, then undergoes hemorrhagic infarction.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because the ovary has a dual supply and twisting may be partial or intermittent.
Paraovarian cysts arise from mesonephric, paramesonephric, or mesothelial remnants in the broad ligament; a separate normal ovary distinguishes them, and torsion or rupture are the complications.
In PCOS, fast GnRH pulses raise LH, LH and insulin drive theca androgen, low FSH limits aromatase, and insulin lowers SHBG, raising free testosterone.
Androgen and AMH arrest small follicles, so no ovulation, no corpus luteum, and no progesterone; the lack of progesterone keeps GnRH pulses fast.

PCOS findings map to androgen excess (hirsutism, acne), anovulation (oligomenorrhea, infertility, endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma), and insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans, diabetes, dyslipidemia).

Tubo-ovarian abscess is a polymicrobial complication of PID in which the inflamed tube adheres to the ovary; rupture causes peritonitis and sepsis, and scarring causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

verify: Size cutoffs vary between sources: the diameter at which a follicle is called a cyst (about 3 cm here) and the mass size that predisposes to torsion (about 5 cm here).

Polycystic ovarian morphology thresholds have changed: Rotterdam 2003 used 12 or more follicles of 2 to 9 mm per ovary or volume above 10 mL, while the 2018 and 2023 international guidelines use 20 or more follicles per ovary with modern transducers. Confirm which definition NABNE expects.
PCOS prevalence (about 6 to 13%) depends on the diagnostic criteria used.

Embryologic origin of the female appendix vesicularis (hydatid of Morgagni) differs between sources (mesonephric in some embryology texts, paramesonephric in some pathology texts), so it was left out of the remnant table.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the term paraovarian or paratubal cyst, and whether it treats tubo-ovarian cyst as a separate entity from hydrosalpinx.
The right-sided predominance of ovarian torsion and its attribution to the sigmoid colon are widely taught but rest on observational data.
